claims.claim: The shear stress profile inside a long microfluidic channel depends only on the pressure gradient along the channel and the channel geometry.
claims.source: The method takes advantage of two physical principles: First, the shear stress profile inside a long microfluidic channel depends only on the pressure gradient along the channel, which can be precisely controlled, and the channel geometry, which is fixed.
claims.evidence: This is a fundamental principle of fluid mechanics applied in the method.

claims.claim: The shear stress profile does not depend on the viscosity of the cell suspension medium.
claims.source: Importantly, the shear stress profile does not depend on the viscosity of the cell suspension medium and smoothly increases from zero at the channel center to a maximum value at the channel walls.
claims.evidence: This is a consequence of the fluid mechanics in the channel geometry and is verified experimentally.

claims.claim: Cells appear circular near the channel center and become increasingly elongated near the channel walls.
claims.source: Accordingly, cells appear circular near the channel center and become increasingly elongated near the channel walls.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: The width of the channel is significantly larger than the cell diameter.
claims.source: As the width of the channel is significantly larger than the cell diameter, fluid shear stresses remain approximately constant across the cell surface, which considerably simplifies the fluid dynamics computations compared to existing microfluidic methods.
claims.evidence: This is a design feature of the experimental setup.

claims.claim: Fluid shear stresses remain approximately constant across the cell surface.
claims.source: As the width of the channel is significantly larger than the cell diameter, fluid shear stresses remain approximately constant across the cell surface, which considerably simplifies the fluid dynamics computations compared to existing microfluidic methods.
claims.evidence: This is a consequence of the channel geometry and is shown in Figure 1f.

claims.claim: Shear-flow induced tank-treading was first theoretically explored by Einstein in 1906.
claims.source: Shear-flow induced tank-treading was first theoretically explored by Einstein, 1906, and was later experimentally observed by H. Schmid-Schönbein et al. in sheared red blood cell suspensions (Schmid-Schöenbein and Wells, 1969; Fischer et al., 1978).
claims.evidence: This is a historical reference supported by citations.

claims.claim: Tank-treading was experimentally observed by H. Schmid-Schönbein et al. in sheared red blood cell suspensions.
claims.source: Shear-flow induced tank-treading was first theoretically explored by Einstein, 1906, and was later experimentally observed by H. Schmid-Schönbein et al. in sheared red blood cell suspensions (Schmid-Schöenbein and Wells, 1969; Fischer et al., 1978).
claims.evidence: This is a historical reference supported by citations.

claims.claim: Tank-treading arises as the flow speed of the suspension fluid in contact with the cell surface facing the channel center is larger compared to the flow speed at the opposite side.
claims.source: Tank-treading arises as the flow speed of the suspension fluid in contact with the cell surface facing the channel center is larger compared to the flow speed at the opposite side.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation of the physical mechanism of tank-treading.

claims.claim: The rotational speed of tank-treading motion increases with increasing shear rate near the channel walls.
claims.source: Hence, the rotational speed of this tank-treading motion increases with increasing shear rate near the channel walls.
claims.evidence: This is observed experimentally and shown in Figure 2j and k.

claims.claim: Tank-treading in combination with the cell's viscous properties leads to energy dissipation.
claims.source: Tank-treading in combination with the cell's viscous properties leads to energy dissipation, which limits the increase of cell strain at higher stresses near the channel walls.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical explanation that is consistent with the observed data.

claims.claim: Most cells have undergone several full rotations before reaching the field of view.
claims.source: Since the microfluidic channel is several centimeters long, most cells, with the exception of those in the center of the channel, have already undergone several full rotations before reaching the field of view.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the channel length and flow conditions.

claims.claim: Cell deformations are in a steady state when measured.
claims.source: Therefore, the cell deformations are in a steady state, which is another major difference compared to existing microfluidic approaches and greatly simplifies the calculation of viscoelastic cell parameters.
claims.evidence: This is a consequence of the long channel and is a key feature of the method.

claims.claim: The Roscoe model assumes that cells behave as a Kelvin-Voigt body consisting of an elastic spring in parallel with a resistive dash-pot element.
claims.source: The Roscoe model assumes that cells behave as a Kelvin-Voigt body consisting of an elastic spring in parallel with a resistive (or viscous) dash-pot element.
claims.evidence: This describes the theoretical model used for analysis.

claims.claim: A commonly used simplified assumption is that the elastic and viscous elements of the Kelvin-Voigt body are constant.
claims.source: A commonly used simplified assumption is that the elastic and viscous elements of the Kelvin-Voigt body are constant (Fregin et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a reference to a common modeling approach in the literature.

claims.claim: Polyacrylamide beads are used to verify the accuracy of the method.
claims.source: Using cell lines and calibrated polyacrylamide beads, we verify that our method provides accurate quantitative measurements of viscoelastic properties.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Measurement results are not or only marginally influenced by the viscosity of the suspension fluid.
claims.source: Measurement results are not or only marginally influenced by experimental details such as the viscosity of the suspension fluid or the time point after suspending the cells.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3f and g.

claims.claim: Measurement results are not or only marginally influenced by the time point after suspending the cells.
claims.source: Measurement results are not or only marginally influenced by experimental details such as the viscosity of the suspension fluid or the time point after suspending the cells.

claims.claim: The cell's viscoelastic properties conform to soft glassy power-law rheology.
claims.source: We demonstrate that the cell's viscoelastic properties measured with our method conform to soft glassy power-law rheology that has been reported for a wide range of cells measured with different methods.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3a and b and discussed in the Results section.

claims.claim: The method can be used for dose-response measurements of drugs that induce actin cytoskeleton disassembly.
claims.source: We also show that our method can be used for dose-response measurements of drugs that induce actin cytoskeleton disassembly, and that these responses are modulated by the cell cycle and the intermediate filament network of the cells.

claims.claim: Drug responses are modulated by the cell cycle.

claims.claim: A neural network detects cells that are in focus at the mid-plane of the microchannel.
claims.source: Using a neural network, we detect cells that are in focus at the mid-plane of the microchannel (Figure 1b), and segment their shapes (Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: This describes the image analysis method used.

claims.claim: The slope of the strain versus stress relationship decreases for higher stress values.
claims.source: In particular, the slope of the strain versus stress relationship decreases for higher stress values.
claims.evidence: This is observed in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: The decrease in slope at higher stress is predominantly due to a dissipative process caused by the tank tread-like motion of the cells.
claims.source: This behavior is predominantly due to a dissipative process caused by the tank tread-like motion of the cells.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the theoretical model.

claims.claim: The tank-treading frequency of a cell is zero at the channel center and increases towards the channel walls.
claims.source: We find that the tank-treading frequency of a cell is zero at the channel center and increases towards the channel walls (Figure 2j and k).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2j and k.

claims.claim: Tank-treading dissipates energy in proportion to the cell's internal viscosity, rotation frequency, and strain.
claims.source: Tank-treading dissipates energy in proportion to the cell's internal viscosity, rotation frequency, and strain.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the Roscoe model.

claims.claim: Energy dissipation limits the cell strain in regions of high shear rate and shear stress.
claims.source: This energy dissipation therefore limits the cell strain in regions of high shear rate and hence shear stress (Figure 2c).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: With increasing loss modulus, cells deform less but align more in flow direction.
claims.source: With increasing loss modulus, cells are also predicted to deform less but to align more in flow direction.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the Roscoe theory.

claims.claim: There is an inverse relationship between stiffness and fluidity, whereby stiffer cells tend to be less fluid-like.
claims.source: Moreover, also in agreement with previous reports, we find an inverse relationship between stiffness and fluidity, whereby stiffer cells tend to be less fluid-like (Fabry et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2005; Lange et al., 2015).

claims.source: Cell fluidity remains constant over this pressure range, but the median stiffness of the cell population increases with increasing pressure by 33% (Figure 3c and d).

claims.claim: The median stiffness of the cell population increases with increasing pressure by 33%.

claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: The latrunculin B dose-response for NIH-3T3 cells agrees with published data obtained using real-time deformability cytometry on HL-60 cells.

claims.claim: NIH-3T3 cells express high levels of the intermediate filament protein vimentin.
claims.source: To explore the attenuated LatB responsiveness of NIH-3T3 fibroblasts compared to HL-60 leukemia cells, we reasoned that NIH-3T3 cells express high levels of the intermediate filament protein vimentin (Figure 7a) that may protect the cells from excessive deformations when filamentous actin is depolymerized.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a.

claims.claim: Vimentin may protect cells from excessive deformations when filamentous actin is depolymerized.
claims.source: To explore the attenuated LatB responsiveness of NIH-3T3 fibroblasts compared to HL-60 leukemia cells, we reasoned that NIH-3T3 cells express high levels of the intermediate filament protein vimentin (Figure 7a) that may protect the cells from excessive deformations when filamentous actin is depolymerized.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the study.

claims.claim: Cytochalasin D binds to the barbed end of filamentous actin and leads to a net depolymerization of the actin cytoskeleton.
claims.source: To test this idea, we measure the stiffness of NIH-3T3 and vimentin-knock-out (vim(-/-)) fibroblasts in response to 30 min treatment with cytochalasin D (2 µM), which binds to the barbed end of filamentous actin and—similar to LatB—leads to a net depolymerization of the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 7a).
claims.evidence: This is a known mechanism of cytochalasin D action.

claims.claim: Cytochalasin D treated vim(-/-) cells soften by a considerably greater extent (2.16-fold) compared to wild-type cells (1.22 fold).
claims.source: We find that cytochalasin D treated vim(-/-) cells soften by a considerably greater extent (2.16-fold) compared to wild-type cells (1.22 fold) (Figure 7b and c), in support of the notion that vimentin stabilizes the cytoskeleton.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b and c.

claims.claim: Vimentin stabilizes the cytoskeleton.
claims.source: We find that cytochalasin D treated vim(-/-) cells soften by a considerably greater extent (2.16-fold) compared to wild-type cells (1.22 fold) (Figure 7b and c), in support of the notion that vimentin stabilizes the cytoskeleton.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claims.source: Desmin, which is the dominant intermediate filament in skeletal muscle, forms an intermediate filament network in fibroblasts that is structurally similar to the vimentin network in wild-type cells (Figure 7a).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about desmin.

claims.claim: Desmin forms an intermediate filament network in fibroblasts that is structurally similar to the vimentin network in wild-type cells.
claims.source: Desmin, which is the dominant intermediate filament in skeletal muscle, forms an intermediate filament network in fibroblasts that is structurally similar to the vimentin network in wild-type cells (Figure 7a).

claims.source: Similar to vimentin-expressing MEFs, vim(-/-) desmin-expressing MEFs also display an attenuated cytochalasin D response (1.37-fold), confirming that both the vimentin and desmin intermediate filament network can protect cells from excessive deformations when filamentous actin is depolymerized (Figure 7c).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7c.

claims.claim: Both the vimentin and desmin intermediate filament network can protect cells from excessive deformations when filamentous actin is depolymerized.
claims.source: Similar to vimentin-expressing MEFs, vim(-/-) desmin-expressing MEFs also display an attenuated cytochalasin D response (1.37-fold), confirming that both the vimentin and desmin intermediate filament network can protect cells from excessive deformations when filamentous actin is depolymerized (Figure 7c).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Larger NIH-3T3 cells tend to be softer compared to smaller cells.
claims.source: In our measurements, we observe that larger NIH-3T3 cells tend to be softer compared to smaller cells (Figure 8a).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8a.

claims.source: We hypothesized that this weak size-dependence of cell stiffness might be attributable to cell cycle progression, which leads to changes in chromatin compaction and cell volume.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the study.

claims.claim: Cell cycle progression leads to changes in chromatin compaction and cell volume.
claims.source: We hypothesized that this weak size-dependence of cell stiffness might be attributable to cell cycle progression, which leads to changes in chromatin compaction and cell volume.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle progression.

claims.claim: Cell radius increases with cell cycle progression.
claims.source: We find as expected that cell radius increases with cell cycle progression (Figure 8d).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8d.

claims.claim: Cell stiffness steadily increases towards the end of the G1 and the beginning of the S-phase.
claims.source: In addition, cell stiffness steadily increases towards the end of the G1 and the beginning of the S-phase, and then rapidly decreases as the cell cycle progresses (Figure 8e).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8e.

claims.claim: Cell stiffness rapidly decreases as the cell cycle progresses after the beginning of S-phase.
claims.source: In addition, cell stiffness steadily increases towards the end of the G1 and the beginning of the S-phase, and then rapidly decreases as the cell cycle progresses (Figure 8e).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8e.

claims.claim: Changes in cell stiffness and cell radius occur at different stages of the cell cycle.
claims.source: When we bin the cells according to their green fluorescent intensities (i.e. according to their cell cycle progression) and plot stiffness versus cell radius (Figure 8f), we find substantially larger and non-monotonic fluctuations of cell stiffness versus cell radius, compared to the smaller, monotonic decrease of cell stiffness in the radius-binned data (Figure 8c). These differences arise because changes in cell stiffness and cell radius occur at different stages of the cell cycle.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Established methods such as atomic force microscopy, micropipette aspirations, or magnetic tweezer microrheology have a relatively low throughput of typically below 10–100 cells/hr.
claims.source: Viscoelastic cell properties can be measured with established methods such as atomic force microscopy (Cordes et al., 2020), micropipette aspirations (Zhelev et al., 1994), or magnetic tweezer microrheology (Bonakdar et al., 2016). These methods have a relatively low throughput of typically below 10–100 cells/hr.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with existing methods based on citations.

claims.claim: The need to measure cell mechanical properties with substantially higher throughput led to the recent development of various microfluidic techniques.
claims.source: The need to measure cell mechanical properties with substantially higher throughput led to the recent development of various microfluidic techniques (Urbanska et al., 2020) including hydrodynamic stretching (Gossett et al., 2012), real-time deformability cytometry (Otto et al., 2015; Fregin et al., 2019), micro-filtration (Rowat et al., 2012), and micro-constriction systems (Lange et al., 2015; Lange et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a review of the field based on citations.

claims.claim: The method uses a simple microfluidic channel with one inlet and outlet, without a flow-focussing geometry.
claims.source: We suspend cells in a medium that is pumped with high pressure (typically 50–300 kPa) through a long, parallel microfluidic channel with one inlet and outlet (no flow-focussing geometry is needed).
claims.evidence: This describes a design feature of the method.

claims.claim: Simple microfluidic channels are commercially available at low cost.
claims.source: Such simple microfluidic channels are commercially available at low cost, which we expect will facilitate a widespread adoption of the technique.
claims.evidence: This is a practical consideration about the method.

claims.claim: The large driving pressure gives rise to sufficiently large (>50 Pa) shear stresses to induce measurable cell deformations.
claims.source: The large driving pressure gives rise to sufficiently large (>50 Pa) shear stresses to induce measurable cell deformations.
claims.evidence: This is a design feature of the method.

claims.claim: The high pressure can be controlled with a simple pressure regulator, without the need for a precise microfluidic controller.
claims.source: The high pressure can be controlled with a simple pressure regulator, without the need for a precise microfluidic controller—another advantage compared to existing methods that typically operate under lower pressure.
claims.evidence: This is a practical advantage of the method.

claims.claim: The large channel diameter prevents clogging due to debris.
claims.source: The width and height of the channel (200 µm) are much larger than the cell diameter, which prevents clogging due to debris that is often encountered in microfluidic constriction-based systems (Lange et al., 2015; Lange et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a practical advantage of the method.

claims.claim: The large channel diameter ensures that fluid shear stresses do not vary appreciably across the cell.
claims.source: Most importantly, the large channel diameter ensures that fluid shear stresses do not vary appreciably across the cell, which simplifies the analysis of cell mechanical properties as the cells do not deform into complex bullet- or hourglass-like shapes as seen in other methods (Lange et al., 2015; Lange et al., 2017; Urbanska et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a design feature that simplifies analysis.

claims.claim: Suspending cells in a fluid with high viscosity achieves a flow speed that is sufficiently low to capture cells without motion blur at a typical exposure time of 30 µs.
claims.source: By suspending the cells in a fluid with high viscosity (typically >1 Pa⋅s), we achieve a flow speed that is sufficiently low (<20 mm/s) so that the cells' speed, position, and shape can be captured without motion blur at a typical exposure time of 30 µs using a standard CMOS-camera mounted to a routine laboratory microscope.
claims.evidence: This is a design feature of the method.

claims.claim: The lateral flow profile in the channel causes a tank-treading-like cell motion, which imposes periodic cell deformations with frequencies on the order of 10 Hz.
claims.source: The lateral flow profile in the channel causes a tank-treading-like cell motion, which imposes periodic cell deformations with frequencies on the order of 10 Hz.
claims.evidence: This is observed experimentally.

claims.claim: At low frequencies and strain rates around 10 Hz, elastic cell properties dominate over viscous cell properties.
claims.source: At such low frequencies and strain rates, elastic cell properties dominate over viscous cell properties (Fabry et al., 2001; Mietke et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The cell transit through the microfluidic channel lasts for several seconds.
claims.source: The cell transit through the microfluidic channel lasts for several seconds, which is much longer than the period time of the cells' tank treading rotation, implying that the measured cell deformations can safely be assumed to have reached a steady-state.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the channel length and flow speed.

claims.claim: Measuring visco-elastic parameters from steady-state cell deformations has a major advantage over existing microfluidic techniques in that no visco-elastic models or pre-conceived response functions are needed.
claims.source: Measuring visco-elastic parameters from steady-state cell deformations has a major advantage over existing microfluidic techniques in that no visco-elastic models (e.g. Maxwell, Voigt etc.) or pre-conceived response functions (e.g. exponential, bi-exponential, power-law etc.) are needed to fit the transient cell deformation responses during the cells' passage through narrow constrictions and channels (Lange et al., 2015; Fregin et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological advantage compared to other techniques.

claims.claim: If an exponential function is fitted to a power-law creep response, the resulting viscoelastic cell properties would largely depend on the time scale of the experiment.
claims.source: If for example an exponential function is fitted to a power-law creep response, the resulting viscoelastic cell properties would largely depend on the time scale of the experiment (e.g. the passage time of the cell through the microfluidic constriction or channel) and less so on the cell's intrinsic mechanical properties (Fabry et al., 2001; Lange et al., 2015; Fregin et al., 2019)
claims.evidence: This is a critique of other methods based on citations.

claims.claim: The values obtained with the shear flow method are not influenced by the time scale of the experiment.
claims.source: By contrast, the values obtained with our method are not influenced by the time scale of the experiment.
claims.evidence: This is an advantage of the steady-state measurement approach.

claims.claim: Once the flow velocity profile is known, viscoelastic properties can be determined from a single image because all cell deformations are in a steady-state.
claims.source: Hence, once the flow velocity profile is known, we can determine the viscoelastic properties from a single image because all cell deformations are in a steady-state.
claims.evidence: This is a consequence of the steady-state measurement approach.

claims.claim: User-friendly software for image acquisition and data analysis is provided and can be downloaded at https://github.com/fabrylab/shear_flow_deformation_cytometer.
claims.source: We provide user-friendly software for image acquisition and data analysis on a standard PC, which can be downloaded at https://github.com/fabrylab/shear_flow_deformation_cytometer (copy archived at swh:1:rev:2d35a697243c432cddd52e10d2e3c5121f922adf; Gerum, 2022).

results.result: The authors developed a shear flow deformation cytometry method using a simple, commercially available microfluidic channel (5.8 cm long, 200 µm wide) where cells suspended in high-viscosity fluid (0.5-10 Pa·s) are pumped at 50-300 kPa pressure. The large channel diameter relative to cell size ensures approximately constant shear stress across cells and prevents clogging, while high viscosity enables imaging without motion blur.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C13-C14, C18-C20, C92-C98 describe the experimental setup and its design advantages. These are well-supported by the Methods section, Figure 1, and are internally consistent. The design features (channel dimensions, pressure range, viscosity) are clearly specified and their advantages (preventing clogging, constant shear stress, no motion blur) are logically justified.

results.result: The method exploits two physical principles: (1) shear stress depends only on pressure gradient and channel geometry, not fluid viscosity, and (2) cells undergo tank-treading rotation due to the flow profile, with rotation frequency increasing toward channel walls. Cells reach steady-state deformation after several rotations before measurement, and at ~10 Hz frequencies, elastic properties dominate over viscous properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17, C23-C27, C99-C101 describe the physical principles underlying the method. These are supported by fluid mechanics theory (Equation 4), experimental observations (Figure 2j-k, Video 1), and citations to prior work (C21-C22, C100). The steady-state assumption is justified by the long channel length relative to rotation period.

results.result: Viscoelastic cell properties are extracted using Roscoe's theoretical framework, which models cells as Kelvin-Voigt bodies (elastic spring in parallel with viscous dashpot) and predicts that cell deformation depends on elastic modulus while alignment depends on loss modulus.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C28, C30, C109, C51 describe the theoretical basis (Roscoe model). This is well-documented with proper citations and mathematical formulations (Equations 10-22). The model assumptions are clearly stated, though limitations are acknowledged (C110-C113).

results.result: Cell shape analysis using neural networks reveals that cell strain increases non-linearly with shear stress, with decreasing slope at higher stress due to energy dissipation from tank-treading. Tank-treading frequency is zero at channel center and increases toward walls, with energy dissipation proportional to cell viscosity, rotation frequency, and strain.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C41-C43, C45-C46 describe cell deformation behavior and its physical interpretation. These are supported by experimental data (Figure 2a-c, j-k) and theoretical explanation based on the Roscoe model. The non-linear stress-strain relationship and its attribution to tank-treading dissipation are consistent with the data.

results.result: Suspended cells exhibit power-law, soft glassy rheological behavior consistent with previous reports: cell stiffness is log-normally distributed, fluidity is normally distributed, and stiffness and fluidity scale inversely. These findings agree with predictions from soft glassy rheology theory.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C35, C55, C114-C118 describe the rheological behavior of cells. These are well-supported by experimental data (Figure 3a-c) and extensive citations to prior work showing similar findings with different methods. The agreement across multiple techniques strengthens the validity.

results.result: Cell stiffness increases by 33% with increasing pressure (100-300 kPa) while fluidity remains constant. This increase is attributed to stress-stiffening rather than shear rate effects, as demonstrated by experiments varying alginate concentration at constant pressure.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57, C59-C60, C120 describe stress-stiffening behavior. The experimental design (varying pressure vs. varying viscosity at constant pressure) effectively isolates stress-stiffening from shear rate effects. Data in Figure 3d-g support the conclusions, though the statistical significance of C59 is explicitly noted as marginal.

results.result: Method accuracy was validated using AFM-calibrated polyacrylamide beads, which showed constant, pressure-independent shear modulus over a 10-fold pressure range (20-200 kPa) and agreement with AFM measurements, demonstrating that Roscoe theory gives quantitatively accurate estimates regardless of pressure and fluid viscosity.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C32, C121-C122, C66 describe validation with polyacrylamide beads. Figure 4 shows good agreement between shear flow cytometry and AFM measurements. The pressure-independence for linear elastic beads (C121) validates the method, while the slight fluidity increase at high strain (C66) is appropriately attributed to poroelastic effects with citation.

results.result: Measurement results are not or only marginally influenced by suspension fluid viscosity or time after cell suspension (stable up to 60 min), demonstrating robustness of the method and validity of Roscoe theory assumptions for living cells in shear-thinning fluids.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34, C61, C119 describe method robustness. These are supported by experimental data (Figure 3f-i) showing minimal effects of alginate concentration and time. This validates key assumptions of the method and demonstrates practical utility.

results.result: The method can estimate rheological properties of the suspension fluid from the flow velocity profile, measuring complex rheology simultaneously with cells under identical conditions. Alginate rheology measured this way agrees closely with cone-plate rheometer measurements (31% deviation over 5 orders of magnitude in shear rate).
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C127 describe the ability to characterize suspension fluid rheology. This is supported by Figure 2d-g showing velocity profiles and viscosity measurements. The agreement with cone-plate rheometry (C127) validates the approach, though 31% deviation is notable.

results.result: The method measures each cell at a single tank-treading frequency depending on channel position, sampling frequency-dependent properties across a population. Tank-treading frequency can be directly measured in some cells or estimated from shear rate using an empirical equation, though this equation may not hold universally for all cell types or fluids.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C133 describe frequency measurement approach. The direct measurement method (C131) is demonstrated in Figure 2h-i, and the empirical estimation (C132, Equation 20) is shown in Figure 2j-k. The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations (C133) regarding generalizability.

results.result: NIH-3T3 cells soften with latrunculin B (EC50=35.2 nM, 1.47-fold max response), agreeing with published RT-DC data. HL-60 cells show similar EC50 (26.4 nM) but much higher maximum response (5.0-fold vs. 1.5-fold in other methods), attributed to lower strain rates (~10 s⁻¹) where elastic properties dominate, unlike high strain rate methods (>100 s⁻¹) where viscous behavior dominates.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73, C135, C137-C138 describe dose-response measurements. The data (Figure 6) support the EC50 values and maximum responses. The explanation for higher sensitivity (lower strain rates) is logical and supported by citations (C137-C138), though direct experimental validation of the strain rate hypothesis is not provided.

results.result: Cell rheological behavior is mediated by interplay between actin and intermediate filaments. Vimentin-knockout cells soften 2.16-fold with cytochalasin D vs. 1.22-fold for wild-type, demonstrating that vimentin stabilizes the cytoskeleton. Desmin-expressing cells show similar protection (1.37-fold), confirming that intermediate filament networks protect cells from excessive deformation when actin is depolymerized.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C38, C74-C82, C139-C143 describe the role of intermediate filaments. The experimental design (comparing wild-type, vimentin-knockout, and desmin-expressing cells) is appropriate, and data (Figure 7) clearly show differential responses to cytochalasin D. Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.05, p<0.01). The findings are consistent with prior literature (C140-C142).

results.result: Cell rheological behavior is cell-cycle-dependent. NIH-3T3 cells stiffen during G1 phase with maximum stiffness at late G1/early S-phase, then soften before G2/M phase. Cell radius increases during G1-to-S transition. Changes in stiffness and radius occur at different cell cycle stages, explaining the weak overall size-dependence of stiffness.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C37, C83-C89, C145-C147 describe cell cycle dependence. The use of Fucci fluorescent reporter (C144) enables cell cycle staging, and data (Figure 8) show clear trends. The interpretation that stiffness and size changes occur at different stages (C89) is supported by Figure 8f. However, the mechanism underlying stiffness changes is not explored.

results.result: Measuring viscoelastic parameters from steady-state deformations has major advantages over existing microfluidic techniques: no viscoelastic models or pre-conceived response functions are needed to fit transient responses, and values are not influenced by experimental time scale. Viscoelastic properties can be determined from a single image once flow velocity profile is known.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 describe methodological advantages. The steady-state approach is well-justified by the long channel and multiple rotations before measurement (C26-C27, C101). The critique of other methods (C103) is supported by citations. The single-image capability (C105) is a logical consequence of steady-state conditions.

results.result: User-friendly software is provided (available on GitHub), though current implementation stores ~4 GB of uncompressed images per experiment and analyzes at ~50 frames/s. The method can be easily and inexpensively implemented on standard microscopes.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108, C150 describe practical implementation. Software availability (C106) is verifiable. Storage requirements (C107) and processing speed (C108) are clearly stated limitations. The claim about easy implementation (C150) is reasonable given the simple channel design and standard microscopy equipment.

results.result: The method has acknowledged limitations: cells deform non-linearly with stress-stiffening, measurements represent effective secant modulus not small-strain tangential modulus, cells are not homogeneous materials, and cells occasionally deform into sigmoidal rather than ellipsoidal shapes at high stress or with cytoskeleton-softening drugs.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C113 acknowledge method limitations. These are appropriately discussed with supporting citations (C110, C112) and experimental observations (C113). The authors transparently address assumptions of the Roscoe model that may not fully apply to living cells.

results.result: Shear flow deformation cytometry provides accurate quantitative measurements of elastic and dissipative cell properties at high throughput, addressing limitations of low-throughput methods (AFM, micropipette aspiration: <10-100 cells/hr). Unlike other high-throughput microfluidic methods, cells are measured under near steady-state conditions at low-to-moderate strain rates where elastic responses dominate.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91, C149, C151 summarize the method's advantages. The throughput advantage over traditional methods (C90) is well-established by citations. The steady-state, low strain rate advantages (C151) are demonstrated throughout the manuscript. The claim of accuracy (C149) is supported by validation experiments (Figure 4-5).

results.result: Cell functions are accompanied by phenotypic changes in viscoelastic properties, and measuring them can elucidate cellular functions in health and disease. For example, neutrophil activation increases cell stiffness, leading to sequestration in lung capillaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C11 provide biological motivation. These are general statements supported by citations to prior work. They establish the importance of measuring cell mechanical properties but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Cell size dependence of stiffness is also detectable in HL-60 and THP1 cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C148 extends the size-dependence observation to other cell types. This is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1, though the data are not extensively discussed.

results.result: Shear stress deformability cytometry can be combined with fluorescent imaging.
results.evaluation: Claim C144 describes a technical capability demonstrated with Fucci cell cycle experiments (Figure 8). This is a straightforward extension showing the method's versatility.
